purpose: Adds WP 6.9+ pluggable overrides for wp_cache_get/set(_multiple)_salted to the Redis object-cache drop-in, plus a stub-based PHP unit test suite for them. The implementation turns out to be functionally identical to WP core's own cache-compat.php fallback, which directly contradicts the PR description's claim of a native 'salt-in-key' performance optimization.
riskRationale: The overrides are behaviorally identical to core's cache-compat.php (same wrapper-at-stable-key + per-read PHP salt comparison), so they introduce no functional/security regression. Risk is limited to: (a) a substantially misleading PR description that claims a performance benefit the code does not deliver, and (b) an entirely redundant override that duplicates core logic and adds long-term maintenance/drift surface in a performance-critical caching drop-in.

text: The two newest open threads are stale: they were written against the PR description's 'salt-in-key' narrative and do not apply to the actually-coded wrapper-at-stable-key implementation (memory is bounded because writes overwrite one stable key, and non-salted wp_cache_delete() continues to work — one of the threads' memory/divergence concerns and the test thread are already resolved by the shipped code and the new test file). The genuine issue flagged in thread 4 stands and is the substance of this review: the PR description misrepresents what the code does, and the override is a 1:1 duplicate of WP core's 6.9 cache-compat.php fallback that gives no performance win while adding drift risk.

reasoning: The overrides exactly duplicate WP core's 6.9 cache-compat.php (same wrapper array, same PHP salt comparison on every read), contradicting the PR's stated 'salt-in-key / native Redis ops / eliminate wrapper encode-decode + salt comparison' claim. There is no performance benefit, and the functions add unnecessary drift surface. This needs a maintainer decision (drop the redundant overrides OR keep strictly as documented compat shims) and an honest PR description before merge.

message: The PR description misrepresents the implementation, and the guidance the current code contradicts the claimed optimization. The description states the drop-in 'embeds the salt directly into the Redis key and stores raw data, eliminating core's wrapper-array (data/salt) encode/decode + PHP salt comparison on every read' via $cache_key.':'.$salt (the 'salt-in-key' Option A). The actual code stores array('data'=>...,'salt'=>...) at the original $cache_key and performs the same $salt !== $cache['salt'] comparison on every read — identical to WP core's cache-compat.php. The stated performance optimization is therefore not delivered, the narrative is misleading, and three open review threads were written against the (never-merged) salt-in-key version.
suggestion: Rewrite the PR description and title to match reality: the change adopts core's wrapper-at-stable-key format and provides zero performance gain over core. Decide concretely between (a) dropping these redundant overrides entirely (core's cache-compat.php already supplies identical behavior for WP 6.9+) or (b) keeping them explicitly as compat shims only, and if kept, use the Decision in code comments that they already make clear. Resolve/re-close the three stale threads against the salt-in-key narrative.

message: The four added functions are behavior-neutral: each is a logically identical re-implementation of WP core's wp_cache_get_salted/wp_cache_set_salted/wp_cache_get_multiple_salted/wp_cache_set_multiple_salted from wp-includes/cache-compat.php (same gate via isset( $cache['salt'], $cache['data'] ) and $salt !== $cache['salt']). Because the drop-in loads first and wins the guarded global, and the functions come in via the explicit function_exists guard, they change nothing versus core and for only *future* drift risk (WP core could evolve this contract). No value over the reference redis-cache plugin, which correctly does not override these at all.
suggestion: Prefer not to ship redundant overrides of cache-compat.php. Unless there is a measured reason the drop-in must intercept these (none is stated), remove the four functions and let core's pluggable fallbacks run unmodified; if kept, state the concrete WP<6.9 robustness rationale in a comment and keep the tests.

message: The three earlier open review threads (still in the PR context) assert problems that do not exist against the merged code: (1) 'unbounded orphaned-key accumulation' applies only to salt-in-key, which is not implemented — wrapper-at-stable-key overwrites the same key so memory stays bounded; (2) 'non-salted wp_cache_delete() can no longer invalidate' also applies only to salt-in-key — the shipped code stores at the original key so plain delete still works (and the added test test_unsalted_delete_invalidates_salted_entry confirms it); (3) 'no tests' is satisfied by the added class-object-cache-test.php. These threads are stale.
suggestion: Close or explicitly mark the three threads addressed/not-applicable to avoid future confusion, and annotate that each was scoped to the unmerged salt-in-key design described in the PR text rather than the shipped wrapper-at-stable.xlsx-key implementation.

message: The new test suite is thorough for the metal: it stubs $wp_object_cache with an in-memory we shim and asserts all real behavioral contract points — set/get same-salt round-trip, mismatched-salt miss, miss-on-empty, single underlying key after multiple writes (proving memory stays bounded), exact stored-wrapper shape, non-salted delete invalidation, get/set_multiple result remapping to original keys, and array-salt normalization including order sensitivity. This directly verifies core's cache-compat contract rather than only mocking the functions' own internals.

Good defensive adherence to WP conventions: each override is wrapped in if ( ! function_exists( ... ) ), signatures strictly match WP 6.9 core (getters $cache_key,$group,$salt; setters with $expire default 0), array salts are normalized with implode( ':', $salt ), expire is cast to (int), and @since:2.2.0 documentation matches the drop-in's internal versioning. The implementation is safe and behaviorally correct even if redundant.
